structure.title: About the Federal Reserve
structure.summary:
iii
About the Federal Reserve
The Federal Reserve was created by an act of Congress on December 23, 1913, to provide the nation with a safer, more flexible, and more stable monetary and financial system. In establishing the Federal Reserve System, the United States was divided geographically into 12 Districts, each with a separately incorporated Reserve Bank.
For more information about the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve System, visit the Board’s website at https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/default.htm. Online versions of the Board’s annual report are available at https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/annual- report/default.htm.

structure.title: 1 Overview
structure.summary: The 2023 Annual Report describes the Federal Reserve’s operations across five core functions: monetary policy, financial stability, financial institution supervision and regulation, payment-system safety and efficiency, and consumer protection and community development. It also explains the System’s structure of 12 Reserve Banks and a seven-member Board of Governors, and provides appendixes covering leadership, FOMC meeting minutes, audited finances and oversight reviews, budgets and currency costs, policy actions, litigation, and historical statistics.

structure.title: 2 Monetary Policy and Economic Developments

nodes.title: March 2024 Summary
Recent Economic and Financial Developments
nodes.summary: The text reviews recent U.S. and international economic and financial developments and monetary policy. U.S. inflation has fallen considerably but remains above target, while long-term expectations are stable. The labor market remains tight despite easing demand, with stronger labor supply and moderating but elevated wage growth. Economic growth was robust in 2023, led by consumers and recovering housing, while business investment and manufacturing weakened. Financial conditions tightened, borrowing costs remained high, and bank lending slowed. The banking system is resilient, but elevated asset valuations, leverage, unrealized asset losses, and funding risks warrant monitoring. Foreign growth weakened, inflation declined unevenly, and many central banks paused tightening or began easing. The FOMC kept its policy rate at 5.25%–5.50% and indicated that cuts would depend on greater confidence in sustainable disinflation.

nodes.title: Monetary Policy
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial stability, international economic and inflation developments, and U.S. monetary policy. It describes a resilient banking system with continuing valuation, leverage, asset-loss, and funding risks; weaker foreign growth and easing but uneven inflation; broadly paused foreign rate hikes and expected 2024 easing; the FOMC’s continued 5.25–5.50 percent policy rate and data-dependent approach toward eventual cuts; ongoing balance-sheet runoff totaling about $1.4 trillion; and a special topic showing that tight labor-market conditions narrowed employment and wage disparities for historically disadvantaged groups, although the discussion is incomplete.

nodes.title: Special Topics
nodes.summary: The text reviews interest-rate developments, the Federal Reserve's 2 percent inflation objective and data-dependent policy approach, and its ongoing balance-sheet runoff under an ample-reserves framework. It also discusses narrowing but persistent employment and earnings disparities, the effects of high mortgage rates and supply constraints on housing, balance-sheet and money-market developments, and monetary policy rules that now generally support federal funds rates close to the current target range.

This section reviews the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy and U.S. and international economic and financial developments through excerpts from its March 2024 and June 2023 reports. Inflation has fallen considerably but remains above 2 percent, while a still-tight labor market, strong 2023 economic growth, and easing but persistent wage and price pressures shape the outlook. It covers weaker business investment and manufacturing, tighter financial conditions, housing constraints, slower bank lending, banking-system resilience and vulnerabilities, and uneven foreign growth and disinflation. The FOMC has held the federal funds rate at 5.25–5.50 percent, continued balance-sheet runoff, and remains committed to returning inflation to 2 percent before reducing rates. Special topics address labor-market disparities, interest-rate and monetary-policy developments, the inflation objective, housing, balance-sheet and money-market conditions, and policy-rate rules.

nodes.title: June 2023 Summary
Recent Economic and Financial Developments
nodes.summary: The June 2023 report describes an economy with moderating but still excessive inflation, a highly tight labor market, and modest growth weakened by tighter financial conditions. The FOMC raised the federal funds rate to 5–5¼ percent and continued balance-sheet reduction, while emphasizing data dependence, policy lags, and its commitment to 2 percent inflation. It reviews easing headline and goods inflation but persistent core services pressures, strong yet cooling employment, slowing consumer and business activity, weakening housing, and tighter credit conditions. Financial stability remained generally resilient despite three bank failures, elevated real-estate valuations, and vulnerabilities among banks and nonbank institutions. International activity recovered temporarily, foreign inflation eased mainly through lower energy prices, and major foreign central banks continued tightening cautiously.

nodes.title: Monetary Policy
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial, international, and U.S. monetary developments. Real estate and debt vulnerabilities remained moderate but elevated, while failures of three banks exposed risks from uninsured deposits, falling long-duration asset values, and weak risk management; the wider banking system remained liquid and capable of absorbing losses, though nonbank leverage and funding risks persisted. Foreign growth rebounded early in 2023, led partly by China, Europe proved resilient, and headline inflation eased while food and core inflation stayed high. Major foreign central banks generally continued tightening, with some urging caution, and the dollar weakened slightly. The FOMC raised the federal funds target to 5–5¼ percent, slowed the pace of increases, and continued reducing securities holdings by about $420 billion, partly offset by bank liquidity support. Labor-market strength narrowed employment and wage disparities but did not eliminate them. Bank credit conditions tightened and were expected to tighten further, potentially weighing unevenly on economic activity, especially in commercial real estate and small businesses. In response to March banking stress, discount-window borrowing rose, the BTFP was introduced, and Federal Reserve lending caused total assets to increase despite ongoing SOMA reduction.

nodes.title: Special Topics
nodes.summary: The text reviews Federal Reserve balance-sheet reduction and its partial offset by banking-system liquidity support, including the effects of the BTFP, discount-window lending, and ON RRP operations on money markets. It describes narrowing but persistent employment and wage disparities across demographic and educational groups, tightening bank credit and its potentially uneven effects—especially on commercial real estate and small businesses—and notes that monetary policy rules called for high policy rates amid above-target inflation and tight labor markets.

The June 2023 summary describes an economy with moderating but still excessive inflation, a highly tight yet cooling labor market, and modest growth constrained by tighter financial and credit conditions. It covers easing headline and goods inflation alongside persistent core services and food pressures; slowing consumption and business activity, weaker housing, and uneven effects on commercial real estate and small firms; and narrowing but continuing employment and wage disparities. The FOMC raised the federal funds rate to 5–5¼ percent, emphasized its 2 percent inflation commitment, data dependence, and policy lags, and continued balance-sheet reduction, while discount-window lending, the BTFP, and ON RRP operations provided liquidity and partly offset runoff. Financial stability remained broadly resilient after three bank failures exposed uninsured-deposit, duration, and risk-management vulnerabilities, though real-estate valuations, nonbank leverage, and funding risks remained. International activity briefly improved, foreign inflation eased mainly through lower energy prices, major central banks continued tightening cautiously, and the dollar weakened modestly; policy rules supported elevated rates under the prevailing inflation and labor-market conditions.

structure.summary: The section reviews Federal Reserve policy and U.S., international, and financial conditions in June 2023 and March 2024. Inflation had fallen substantially but remained above 2 percent, while economic growth was strong earlier and then moderated, labor markets stayed tight but cooled, and wage, service-price, and food pressures persisted. It covers weaker consumption, investment, manufacturing, housing, bank lending, commercial real estate, and small firms amid tighter financial conditions; banking resilience alongside vulnerabilities involving deposits, duration risk, risk management, real estate, nonbanks, and funding; and uneven foreign growth, disinflation, central-bank tightening, and dollar movements. The FOMC raised rates to 5–5¼ percent, later held them at 5.25–5.50 percent, continued balance-sheet runoff, used liquidity facilities and money-market operations, and maintained its commitment to 2 percent inflation while emphasizing data dependence and policy lags. Special topics address labor disparities, the inflation objective, housing, balance-sheet and money-market conditions, and policy-rate rules.

structure.title: 3 Financial Stability

nodes.title: Monitoring Financial Vulnerabilities
Asset Valuation Pressures
nodes.summary: The text explains the Federal Reserve’s framework for monitoring financial stability, distinguishing unpredictable shocks from accumulating vulnerabilities and describing quarterly assessments that inform policy and coordination with other regulators. It discusses the Financial Stability Report and then focuses on asset valuation pressures and borrowing risks. In 2023, equity, residential and commercial real estate, and farmland valuations remained elevated in various ways, while corporate spreads were relatively moderate. It explains how leverage, opaque risks, limited transactions, and high indebtedness can magnify losses and financial shocks, and provides supporting figures, data definitions, and report citations.

nodes.title: Borrowing by Households and Businesses
nodes.summary: The text assesses financial stability in 2023, finding elevated equity, residential real estate, commercial real estate, and farmland valuations, while corporate spreads were comparatively moderate. It explains how excessive household and business debt can amplify shocks, but notes that aggregate private credit relative to GDP fell to a two-decade low. Businesses generally maintained strong debt-servicing capacity despite high leverage and interest rates, although credit quality weakened slightly and opaque private credit grew rapidly. Household debt and GDP declined, balance sheets remained resilient, and modest increases in consumer delinquencies reflected the end of pandemic support more than looser lending. Banks remained well capitalized overall, but the SVB-related runs highlighted risks from unrealized asset losses and fragile funding; fair-value losses, commercial real estate exposure, and weaker diversification leave some smaller banks vulnerable.

nodes.title: Leverage in the Financial System
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial stability in 2023, covering rapid but opaque private-credit growth; declining household leverage, debt composition, and modestly rising consumer delinquencies; the resilience and vulnerabilities of banks, insurers, and hedge funds; and banking liquidity and interest-rate risks. It describes how the SVB-related crisis was contained by emergency measures, notes remaining exposures to fair-value losses and commercial real estate, and reports that banks maintained strong capital and historically ample liquidity despite some deterioration. It also discusses the continued expansion of money market and other cash-management funds and related SEC reforms. Two figures document bank capital ratios and liquid-asset levels from 2001–23, including group definitions, measurement notes, recession periods, and Federal Reserve data sources.

nodes.title: Funding Risk
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial stability risks outside and within the banking sector. Life insurers increased exposure to risky assets, hedge-fund leverage remained elevated amid growth in the Treasury basis trade, and banks retained ample though somewhat reduced liquidity while maintaining historically high liquid-asset levels and elevated interest-rate exposure; the BTFP ended in March 2024. It describes liquid-asset trends by bank category, expanding money market and other cash-management funds, SEC money market reforms, orderly mutual-fund bond redemptions, and the systemic risks posed by stablecoins. It then outlines Federal Reserve cooperation with domestic and international institutions and explains the FSOC’s structure, responsibilities, 2023 priorities, and monitoring efforts concerning hedge funds and nonbank mortgage servicers.

The section explains how the Federal Reserve monitors financial stability through quarterly assessments of four key vulnerabilities—asset valuations, household and business borrowing, financial-sector leverage, and funding risk—and how this work informs policy, research, regulatory coordination, and the Financial Stability Report. It describes the interdependence of financial institutions and the nonfinancial sector and the importance of a system’s ability to continue providing credit and payment services after shocks. For 2023, it evaluates elevated equity, real estate, and farmland valuations; moderate corporate spreads; household and business debt and credit quality; resilient but exposed household, business, and bank balance sheets; and risks from leverage, opaque private credit, commercial real estate, interest rates, unrealized losses, and limited diversification. It also reviews the SVB-related banking turmoil and emergency response, the resilience and vulnerabilities of banks, insurers, and hedge funds, liquidity and funding conditions, money market and cash-management funds, SEC reforms, mutual-fund redemptions, stablecoins, and nonbank financial risks. The section concludes with Federal Reserve and FSOC cooperation and oversight activities and provides supporting figures, definitions, historical data, measurement notes, sources, and citations.

nodes.title: Domestic and International Cooperation and Coordination
Financial Stability Oversight Council Activities
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 developments in financial stability and cooperation. Mutual funds reduced corporate-bond holdings amid orderly redemptions, while sizable and lightly regulated stablecoin markets remained a potential source of short-term funding stress and crypto-related spillovers. It explains the Federal Reserve’s domestic and international coordination, focusing on the FSOC’s mandate, membership, systemic-risk responsibilities, four 2023 priorities, monitoring of nonbanks, Treasury-market resilience, climate risks, digital assets, new risk-assessment and nonbank-designation frameworks, and its annual report’s findings and featured topics. It also describes the Federal Reserve’s participation in the FSB and the FSB’s 2023 work on open-end fund liquidity mismatches, crypto-asset intermediaries, and nonbank financial resilience.

Financial Stability Board Activities
In light of the interconnected global financial system and the global activities of large U.S. finan- cial institutions, the Federal Reserve participates in international bodies, such as the FSB. The FSB monitors the global financial system and promotes international financial stability by coordi- nating with national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies on information exchanges and work focused on developing strong global financial-sector policies.
In 2023, the FSB engaged in many issues related to global financial stability. Specific work included addressing structural vulnerabilities from liquidity mismatch in open-end funds, assessing the financial stability implications of multifunction crypto-asset intermediaries, and enhancing the resilience of nonbank financial intermediation.

The section explains the Federal Reserve’s domestic and international cooperation on financial stability through the FSOC and FSB. It covers 2023 risks and developments involving mutual funds, stablecoins, nonbanks, Treasury markets, climate, and digital assets; the FSOC’s mandate, priorities, frameworks, and annual report; and the FSB’s global coordination and work on open-end fund liquidity, crypto-asset intermediaries, and nonbank financial resilience.

structure.summary: This section describes how the Federal Reserve monitors and addresses risks to financial stability through vulnerability assessments, stress-test and policy decisions, supervision, research, and cooperation with domestic and international authorities. It evaluates 2023 risks involving valuations, borrowing, leverage, funding, credit and balance sheets, commercial real estate, interest rates, unrealized losses, and financial-sector interconnectedness; discusses the SVB-related banking turmoil and emergency response; and reviews banks, insurers, hedge funds, funds, stablecoins, and other nonbanks, including liquidity and regulatory issues. It also covers FSOC and FSB coordination on systemic risks involving mutual funds, Treasury markets, climate, digital assets, crypto intermediaries, open-end-fund liquidity, and nonbank resilience, with supporting data and technical documentation.

structure.title: 4 Supervision and Regulation

nodes.title: Box 4.1. Banking Sector Conditions
nodes.summary: This section describes the Federal Reserve’s supervision and regulation role in promoting a safe, sound, and efficient financial system that supports the U.S. economy. It supervises financial institutions, develops regulatory policies and handles banking-organization applications, and monitors banking trends through data collection and analysis. Banking-sector conditions are reported semiannually to Congress in the Supervision and Regulation Report. The section also identifies the principal types and numbers of entities supervised by the Federal Reserve, led by bank holding companies, and explains the purpose of Edge Act and agreement corporations.

nodes.title: Supervised and Regulated Institutions
State Member Banks
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s portfolio-based supervision framework and reports 2023 statistics on Federal Reserve member banks, emphasizing the number and share of state member banks, their branches, and their proportion of U.S. commercial banks and assets. Table 4.1 classifies institutions into LISCC, LFBO, RBO, CBO, and insurance/commercial SLHC portfolios, gives their definitions, institution counts, asset totals, SMB subsets, subgroup breakdowns, and footnote details on holding-company coverage.

nodes.title: Bank Holding Companies
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 statistics on U.S. bank holding companies, financial holding companies, and savings and loan holding companies, including their numbers, ownership, asset sizes, activities, and regulatory oversight. It also describes Federal Reserve supervision of insurance-focused SLHCs and implementation of a new risk-based insurance supervisory framework, and introduces financial market utilities as operators of multilateral systems for transferring, clearing, and settling financial transactions.

nodes.title: Savings and Loan Holding Companies
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 statistics on U.S. bank holding companies, financial holding companies, and savings and loan holding companies, including their numbers, ownership, asset levels, classifications, activities, and regulators. It also describes Federal Reserve supervision of insurance-focused SLHCs and implementation of a new risk-based insurance supervisory framework, and introduces financial market utilities as systems that facilitate the transfer, clearing, and settlement of financial transactions.

nodes.title: Financial Market Utilities
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 supervision and regulation statistics for U.S. BHCs, FHCs, SLHCs, insurance-focused holding companies, FMUs, and international banking operations. It describes their numbers, assets, ownership and regulatory classifications; explains the Federal Reserve’s insurance supervisory framework and implementation; outlines FMU supervision, systemic designations, Regulation HH requirements, and interagency coordination; and details foreign branches of U.S. banks, Edge Act and agreement corporations, and U.S. operations and market share of foreign banks.

nodes.title: International Activities
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve oversight of designated and other financial market utilities, including Dodd-Frank responsibilities and Regulation HH requirements, followed by 2023 international banking activities and examination statistics. It outlines risk-based supervisory methods and priorities, discusses the Federal Reserve’s response to the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank and the resulting push for faster, more agile, forward-looking supervision, and reports examination and inspection totals for domestic banking organizations.

The section surveys the institutions supervised and regulated by the Federal Reserve, covering state member banks, bank and savings and loan holding companies, insurance-focused organizations, financial market utilities, and international banking operations. It presents 2023 data on their numbers, assets, ownership, activities, classifications, branches, market shares, and regulatory coverage; explains portfolio-based bank supervision and the risk-based framework for insurance organizations; describes FMU systemic designations, Regulation HH requirements, Dodd-Frank responsibilities, and interagency coordination; and reviews international operations, examination and inspection activity, supervisory priorities, and reforms prompted by the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.

nodes.title: Supervisory Developments
Supervisory and Regulatory Initiatives
Specialized Examinations
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s specialized supervisory examinations and its capital-planning and stress-testing framework, including 2023 results, capital-buffer requirements, the exploratory market shock, related publications, and the scope of the global market shock. It reports 2023 examination totals for fiduciary activities, transfer agents, government securities, and municipal securities; explains oversight of securities-credit lenders under Regulation U; and emphasizes operational resilience, information technology, cybersecurity, and third-party risk management, for which the Federal Reserve provides supervisory guidance and resources.

nodes.title: Operational Resilience, Information Technology, and Cybersecurity
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 supervisory work involving fiduciary activities, transfer agents, government and municipal securities, and securities-credit lenders, including examination counts, regulatory responsibilities, and Regulation U oversight. It then describes operational-resilience, IT, cybersecurity, and third-party-risk supervision; interagency guidance and educational sessions; examinations of financial institutions and technology providers; domestic, private-sector, and international collaboration on cyber resilience, cloud adoption, and incident reporting; and resulting Financial Stability Board publications. Finally, it details the new Novel Activities Supervision Program for crypto-assets, distributed-ledger technology, and technology-driven nonbank partnerships, along with a joint regulatory statement identifying major risks associated with crypto-assets and crypto-sector participants.

nodes.title: Crypto-Asset Supervision
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve's 2023 supervisory initiatives concerning operational, crypto-asset, novel-technology, and climate-related risks. It describes related international risk-management and cyber-reporting publications; the launch and objectives of the Novel Activities Supervision Program; interagency warnings about crypto risks, liquidity volatility, and the process for state member banks to obtain supervisory nonobjection for certain dollar-token activities; the pilot climate scenario analysis exercise; and final climate-risk management principles for large institutions. It concludes by introducing the Federal Reserve's enforcement authority over supervised institutions and affiliated parties for unsafe practices and violations of law or regulation.

nodes.title: Climate-Related Financial Risks
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve supervisory developments involving crypto-asset activities, including liquidity-risk concerns and the process for state member banks to obtain supervisory nonobjection before engaging in certain dollar-token activities. It then discusses the Board’s exploratory 2023 climate scenario analysis exercise and finalized climate-related financial-risk management principles for institutions with at least $100 billion in assets, covering governance, planning, risk management, reporting, scenario analysis, and integration with traditional risk areas. Finally, it introduces the Federal Reserve’s enforcement authority over supervised institutions and affiliated parties for unsafe practices and legal or regulatory violations, including cease-and-desist orders.

nodes.title: Enforcement Actions
nodes.summary: The text covers Federal Reserve supervision and regulation of crypto-asset activities, including liquidity concerns and the supervisory nonobjection process for dollar-token activities; climate-related financial-risk scenario analysis and management principles for large institutions; enforcement authority, 2023 enforcement statistics, penalties, action types, and public disclosure; financial-reporting obligations of certain state member banks; and the Board’s two-level internal appeals process for material supervisory determinations, with the excerpt detailing the initial review.

nodes.title: Internal Appeals of Material Super visory Determinations
nodes.summary: The text reports the Federal Reserve’s 2023 enforcement, disclosure, supervisory appeals, assessment, and training activities. It details formal and informal enforcement actions, civil penalties and their disposition, public availability of enforcement orders, state member bank disclosure requirements, the two-stage appeals process and its 2023 cases, supervision and regulation assessments transferred to the Treasury, and international and minority-depository-institution training and technical assistance. It also notes 20 international training seminars, about 900 foreign participants, collaboration with the IMF and World Bank, and additional training partners, with the source ending before that list is completed.

nodes.title: Assessments for Supervision and Regulation
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s MSD appeals process and reports one appeal and one filing extension in 2023. It explains supervision and regulation assessments for large banking organizations and FSOC-designated nonbank financial companies, including the transfer of $771.1 million collected from 53 institutions to the U.S. Treasury. It also covers the Federal Reserve’s training, technical assistance, and industry outreach, especially its 2023 international supervisory programs, which included 20 seminars for approximately 900 foreign supervisors and collaboration with the IMF, World Bank, and other partners.

nodes.title: Training and Technical Assistance
International Training and Technical Assistance
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s MSD appeals process and 2023 appeal activity; supervision and regulation assessments, including eligibility, Treasury treatment, and 2023 collections; international supervisory training and technical assistance; and support for minority-owned depository institutions through the Partnership for Progress. It covers the program’s statutory basis, resources, staffing and MDI portfolio, 2023 training partnerships, outreach events, conferences, and related policy and statutory references.

nodes.title: Efforts to Support Minority-Owned Depository Institutions
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s domestic and international supervisory work in 2023. Domestically, it explains the Partnership for Progress program and related legal requirements for supporting minority depository institutions, including technical assistance, resources, outreach events, webinars, conferences, the 16-bank MDI portfolio, and programs such as ECIP. Internationally, it outlines the Federal Reserve’s participation in the Financial Stability Board and other standard-setting organizations, highlighting 2023 priorities involving cross-border payments, crypto-assets, open-ended funds, and third-party risk, as well as selected FSB publications on these issues.

The section covers the Federal Reserve’s MSD appeals process and 2023 activity; supervision and regulation assessments and collections; international supervisory training and technical assistance; and domestic and international efforts to support minority-owned depository institutions through the Partnership for Progress and related programs such as ECIP. It also describes the applicable statutory and legal requirements, program resources, staffing and MDI portfolio, 2023 partnerships and outreach activities, and the Federal Reserve’s participation in international standard-setting, including 2023 priorities and FSB publications on cross-border payments, crypto-assets, open-ended funds, and third-party risk.

nodes.title: International Engagement
Financial Stability Board
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve supervisory and regulatory outreach through PFP, including participation in the National Bankers Association conference, a Bank Term Funding Program webinar, and ECIP technical assistance for MDIs and CDFIs. It then reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 international engagement through the FSB and BCBS, highlighting efforts to promote global financial stability, supervisory cooperation, Basel III implementation, responses to banking turmoil, financial digitalization, and emerging risks. It lists major 2023 FSB publications on decentralized finance, commodities markets, crypto-assets, non-bank leverage, cross-border payments, third-party risk, and open-ended funds, and BCBS publications on risk data, climate-related risks, technical amendments, and the 2023 banking turmoil, while noting the BCBS’s membership and role.

nodes.title: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 international supervisory and financial-infrastructure work. It lists key FSB publications on non-bank leverage, cross-border payments, third-party risk, and open-ended-fund liquidity mismatch, then outlines BCBS priorities and final and consultative publications concerning Basel III, banking turmoil, risk management, climate and cryptoasset disclosures, and supervisory principles. It also explains the BCBS’s membership and purpose, and summarizes the Federal Reserve’s CPMI participation, including practical efforts to improve cross-border payments, coordination with IOSCO on central-counterparty losses, margining, and infrastructure principles, and a joint publication on multilateral cross-border payment platforms.

nodes.title: Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 international supervisory and regulatory engagement. It lists selected BCBS publications and consultations, describes CPMI’s work with the FSB and IOSCO to improve cross-border payments and financial-market infrastructure, identifies major CPMI publications and a consultative paper, and explains the Federal Reserve’s IAIS participation, including 2023 progress on insurance capital standards, supervisory principles, climate-risk guidance, and policyholder protection schemes. Links to the relevant publication catalogs and documents are provided.

nodes.title: International Association of Insurance Supervisors
nodes.summary: The text lists major 2023 CPMI publications and a consultative document on payment systems, along with links to complete publication catalogs. It describes the Federal Reserve’s participation in IAIS insurance-standard development, 2023 IAIS initiatives and publications, and the advisory work of IPAC on capital standards, insurer liquidity, and climate risk. It also explains the interagency Shared National Credit program, its governing agencies, review schedule, and sources for further information.

The section describes the Federal Reserve's domestic outreach and 2023 international engagement through the FSB, BCBS, CPMI, and IAIS. It covers initiatives to strengthen global financial stability, supervisory cooperation, Basel III implementation, responses to banking turmoil, digitalization, climate and emerging risks, and insurance oversight. It catalogs key publications and consultations on crypto-assets, decentralized finance, non-bank leverage, cross-border payments, third-party risk, open-ended funds, banking and insurance capital, risk management, and financial-market infrastructure. It also details CPMI and IOSCO efforts on payment systems, central counterparties, margining, and cross-border payment platforms; IAIS and IPAC work on insurance standards, liquidity, climate risk, and policyholder protection; and the Shared National Credit program, while providing publication and informational resources.

nodes.title: Shared National Credit Program
nodes.summary: The text lists key 2023 IAIS consultations and guidance on insurance capital, valuation, capital adequacy, aggregation-method comparability, and climate risk, with links to the documents and the IAIS publications page. It describes the Federal Reserve’s IPAC role, legal basis, 2023 activities on international insurance standards, life-insurer liquidity, and climate issues. It also introduces the interagency Shared National Credit program, identifying its purpose, participating agencies, review schedule, and related information link.

nodes.title: Bank Secrecy Act and Anti-Money-Laundering Compliance
nodes.summary: In 2023, the Federal Reserve continued supervising BSA/AML compliance, helping revise the FFIEC examination manual, implementing the AML Act of 2020, and participating in the Treasury-led BSA Advisory Group. It also coordinated internationally on sanctions, money laundering, and counter-terrorism financing; monitored sanctions related to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine; contributed to FATF standards; and supported FSB work resulting in the 2023 G20 cross-border-payments progress report.

nodes.title: International Coordination on Sanctions, Anti-Money-Laundering, and Counter-Terrorism Financing
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 BSA/AML compliance supervision, interagency manual updates, implementation of the AML Act of 2020, and participation in the Treasury-led BSA Advisory Group. It covers international coordination on sanctions, AML, and counter-terrorism financing through the FATF, FSB, BIS/BCBS, and country-level dialogues and training, including monitoring sanctions linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and supporting the G20 cross-border payments roadmap. It also explains the purpose and scope of Federal Reserve regulatory reporting and details 2023 revisions to the FR Y-7Q report, including new asset reporting requirements, shortened filing deadlines, clarifications, effective dates, and the types of holding companies covered.

The section reviews the Federal Reserve’s supervisory and regulatory framework, 2023 examination and inspection activity, and five-year institution and asset statistics; explains supervision of financial condition, governance, controls, compliance, consumer protection, operational and cyber resilience, technology, third-party relationships, and specialized securities and fiduciary activities; and details the response to the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank. It covers capital planning, stress testing, crypto-asset and novel-technology supervision, climate-risk scenario analysis and management principles, enforcement actions, supervisory appeals, assessments, reporting obligations, and regulatory reporting revisions. It also describes training, technical assistance, minority-depository-institution outreach, international supervisory cooperation and standard-setting across banking, payments, insurance, climate, crypto, financial-market infrastructure, and emerging risks; the Shared National Credit program; and BSA/AML, sanctions, and counter-terrorism-financing oversight, including related domestic, international, FATF, FSB, and G20 initiatives.

nodes.title: Regulatory Reports
Federal Reserve Regulatory Reports
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s international AML/CFT cooperation and training, its regulatory-reporting requirements and the purposes of those reports, detailed 2023 revisions to Federal Reserve and FFIEC reporting forms with their effective dates, and the statutory reviews underlying several changes. It concludes with the Federal Reserve’s supervisory staff-development program for nearly 4,200 professionals and state-agency personnel, while citing related legal authorities and reporting-form resources.

nodes.title: FFIEC Regulatory Reports
nodes.summary: The text describes regulatory-reporting revisions finalized in late 2023, the FFIEC’s role in requiring uniform reports for financial supervision and financial-system assessment, 2023 changes to the Call Reports and FFIEC 002—including data-item consolidation and improved monitoring of hedging and country exposures—and the Federal Reserve’s staff development program for supervisory personnel and state banking agencies. It also provides the FFIEC reporting-forms website and supporting legal and Federal Register citations.

The section covers Federal Reserve and FFIEC regulatory reporting requirements, their supervisory and financial-system purposes, international AML/CFT cooperation and training, and detailed late-2023 revisions to reporting forms—including effective dates, statutory bases, consolidated data items, and improved monitoring of hedging and country exposures. It also describes the FFIEC's uniform-reporting role, the Federal Reserve's supervisory staff-development program for nearly 4,200 professionals and state-agency personnel, and provides related reporting-form resources and legal and Federal Register citations.

nodes.title: Staff Development Programs
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 revisions to Federal Reserve and FFIEC regulatory reporting, including Call Report and FFIEC 002 changes effective September 30, 2023, and other revisions effective June 30, 2024. It explains the purpose and statutory basis of uniform FFIEC reports, summarizes supervisory staff training and its delivery formats, outlines the three-track examiner commissioning program and its 74 successful candidates, and describes continuing professional development resources for Federal Reserve and state examiners.

The section surveys Federal Reserve and FFIEC supervision, regulation, examinations, and reporting, covering institutional and asset trends; oversight of financial condition, governance, compliance, consumer protection, resilience, technology, third parties, securities, fiduciary activities, crypto-assets, climate risks, and emerging threats; and responses to the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures. It also addresses capital and stress testing, enforcement and appeals, assessments, BSA/AML and sanctions, domestic and international cooperation and standard-setting, the Shared National Credit program, minority-institution outreach, and supervisory assistance. In addition, it explains regulatory-reporting purposes, requirements, legal bases, resources, and 2023–2024 form revisions, including Call Report and FFIEC 002 changes and enhanced hedging and country-exposure data. Finally, it describes Federal Reserve and state-examiner training, commissioning, staff development, and continuing professional education.

nodes.title: Regulatory Developments
Rulemakings and Guidance
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s regulatory responsibilities and summarizes its 2023 rulemakings, statements, guidance, and supervisory initiatives. These covered crypto-asset and liquidity risks, stress testing, the Silicon Valley Bank supervision review, LIBOR transition, supervisory technology, valuation practices, third-party risk, commercial real estate, capital and liquidity requirements, resolution planning, novel banking activities and dollar tokens, CRA rules, climate-related risks, interchange fees, consumer-protection thresholds, payment services, reserve requirements, investment-fund and beneficial-ownership reporting, and other interagency policies. It also reports that the Federal Reserve acted on 752 banking applications in 2023 and explains the availability of semiannual application reports, public decision and filing notices, and application guidance on its website.

nodes.title: Banking Applications
nodes.summary: The text continues a 2023 supervision and regulation table, summarizing regulatory announcements and guidance issued between November 13 and December 21, including lending and leasing thresholds, Federal Reserve payment-service pricing, a comment-period extension for large-bank long-term-debt requirements, reserve requirement indexing, Regulation O and FDIC reporting guidance, CRA asset-size thresholds, and beneficial-ownership information guidance. It also explains the Federal Reserve’s banking-application review responsibilities, notes that 752 applications were acted on in 2023, identifies its semiannual applications activity report, and directs readers to online resources for Federal Reserve decisions, filings, and application guidance.

nodes.title: Public Notice of Federal Reserve Decisions and Filings Received
nodes.summary: The text lists Federal Reserve and interagency regulatory actions issued from November 13 through December 21, 2023, covering appraisal exemptions, truth-in-lending and leasing thresholds, payment-service pricing, long-term-debt requirements, reserve requirements, Regulation O and FDIC reporting, Community Reinvestment Act thresholds, and beneficial-ownership information access. It also explains the Federal Reserve's review of banking applications, noting 752 actions in 2023, identifies its semiannual application-activity reports, and directs readers to online resources for regulatory decisions, announcements, and application guidance.

The section reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 regulatory and supervisory work, covering a broad range of financial, banking, consumer-protection, risk-management, capital, liquidity, payments, reporting, and interagency policy matters. It highlights announcements and guidance issued from November 13 through December 21, including threshold adjustments, payment-service pricing, long-term-debt and reserve requirements, Regulation O and FDIC reporting, CRA rules, appraisal exemptions, and beneficial-ownership information. It also explains the Federal Reserve’s banking-application review function, notes 752 applications acted on in 2023, and identifies its semiannual reports and online sources for decisions, filings, notices, and application guidance.

structure.summary: This section describes the Federal Reserve’s supervision and regulation of the U.S. financial system, including the institutions and financial market utilities it oversees, their 2023 conditions and activities, supervisory frameworks, international operations, systemic-risk responsibilities, and interagency coordination. It covers examinations and supervisory priorities involving financial condition, governance, compliance, consumer protection, resilience, technology, third parties, securities, fiduciary activities, crypto-assets, climate risks, capital, stress testing, enforcement, BSA/AML, sanctions, and responses to the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures. It also addresses regulatory reporting requirements and revisions, examiner training and professional development, outreach and supervisory assistance, and the Federal Reserve’s 2023 regulatory actions on banking, consumer, risk, capital, liquidity, payments, and reporting matters. Finally, it explains bank-application reviews, including 752 applications acted on in 2023, and the reports and online resources available for regulatory decisions and filings.

structure.title: 5 Payment System and Reserve Bank Oversight

nodes.title: Payment Services to Depository and Other Institutions
Commercial Check-Collection Service
nodes.summary: The 2023 Annual Report describes the Reserve Banks' priced payment services and their consolidation under Federal Reserve Financial Services, including the launch of FedNow® in July 2023. It details the commercial check-collection service, which offers electronic and paper processing and recovered 102.9 percent of costs in 2023, generating $4.4 million in net income despite declining check volumes and values. It also introduces the commercial ACH service for domestic and cross-border batch payments with same-day or next-day settlement, and defines the depository institutions that use these services.

nodes.title: Commercial Automated Clearinghouse Service
nodes.summary: Reserve Banks offer a range of priced payment and settlement services, now managed through the integrated Federal Reserve Financial Services organization, which was reorganized in anticipation of changing financial services and the FedNow launch. The text describes the commercial check-collection service, including its processing options, 2023 cost recovery, revenue, expenses, income, transaction volume, value, and expected decline, and introduces the commercial ACH service for domestic and cross-border batched payments with same-day or next-day settlement. It also defines depository institutions and notes their economic and payment-system roles.

nodes.title: Box 5.1. Priced Services and Cost Recovery
FedNow Service
nodes.summary: The text presents 2021–23 activity and cost-recovery data for Federal Reserve priced services, including checks, ACH, Fedwire funds, national settlement, and securities transfers, with definitions of the activity measures and a note that Treasury securities entered the priced securities-service totals in 2023. It reports 2023 commercial ACH performance and finances, introduces the July 2023 launch, purpose, adoption, investment, and expected growth of the FedNow instant-payments service, and describes the finances and operations of Fedwire Funds and the National Settlement Service. It also explains the functions and 2023 activity of Fedwire Funds, National Settlement, and the Fedwire Securities Service.

nodes.title: Fedwire Funds and National Settlement Services
nodes.summary: The text reviews Federal Reserve payment-system investments, oversight, costs, revenues, and activity. It reports the $545 million FedNow implementation investment and its technology and outreach components, 2023 cost recovery and financial results for Fedwire Funds and National Settlement Services, and operational statistics for the Fedwire Funds Service and National Settlement Service, including transaction volumes, values, files, and year-over-year changes. It also introduces the Fedwire Securities Service as a real-time securities depository and settlement system for eligible government and related securities, although its description is incomplete in the excerpt.

nodes.title: Fedwire Securities Service
nodes.summary: The text reports the Federal Reserve’s $545 million FedNow implementation investment and plans for future volume reporting, then reviews the 2023 performance of Fedwire Funds, NSS, and Fedwire Securities. It explains each service’s purpose, activity and value changes, cost recovery, revenues, expenses, and net income, along with Fedwire Securities’ expanded 2023 priced-service scope, securities holdings, outstanding issues, and principal and interest payments. It also describes FedLine Solutions as the six connectivity options institutions use to access Reserve Bank services, including their fee structure, cost allocation, and security, connectivity, and contingency roles.

nodes.title: FedLine Solutions: Access to Reserve Bank Services
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 activity and financial results for the Fedwire Securities Service, including its expanded priced scope to Treasury securities, major increases in transfers, payment flows, securities held, and securities outstanding. It describes FedLine Solutions as six access options for Reserve Bank services and notes the shift from legacy to modern products. It then explains Federal Reserve intraday credit and daylight overdrafts, their role in payment efficiency and risk reduction, and their historically low use and fees due to ample reserves, high overnight balances, and free collateralized credit, with a figure documenting trends from 2007–23.

nodes.title: Federal Reserve Intraday Credit
nodes.summary: The text discusses legacy payment-product changes and Federal Reserve oversight of intraday credit, or daylight overdrafts. It defines daylight overdrafts, explains their role in facilitating payments and reducing risk, and reports that their use and associated fees remained low during 2007–2023 because institutions held substantial overnight reserves. Fees are expected to stay low under the ample-reserves regime, especially following the 2011 elimination of charges for collateralized overdrafts. Federal Reserve policy provides no-cost collateralized intraday credit to healthy institutions and is expected to continue limiting demand for such credit.

This section explains the Federal Reserve’s statutory cost-recovery framework for priced payment and settlement services, including the PSAF, 2014–23 financial results, 2023 full cost recovery, accounting adjustments, and the special long-run recovery timeline for FedNow. It reviews the activity, functions, finances, investments, adoption, and operational performance of ACH, checks, FedNow, Fedwire Funds, National Settlement, and Fedwire Securities, including the latter’s expanded Treasury-securities scope in 2023. It also describes FedLine’s six service-access options and their fees, cost allocation, security, and contingency roles, and explains intraday credit and daylight overdrafts, their payment-system benefits, historically low use and fees under ample reserves, and the continuing policy of free collateralized credit for healthy institutions.

The section surveys the Reserve Banks’ priced payment and settlement services, their organization under Federal Reserve Financial Services, and the introduction of FedNow®. It details commercial check and ACH services, including processing, settlement, users, activity, revenues, expenses, and cost recovery. It also explains the statutory pricing and recovery framework, reviews the operations and finances of major payment services, describes FedLine access and security arrangements, and covers intraday credit and daylight overdrafts, including their system benefits, low use under ample reserves, and continued free collateralized availability for healthy institutions.

nodes.title: Currency and Coin
Banknote Development
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s role in issuing and distributing U.S. currency, its 2023 note and coin circulation statistics, and efforts to modernize the Currency Program and develop the next generation of banknotes. It reports declines in note distributions, receipts, and net payments, continued growth in currency outstanding driven mainly by $100-note demand, and increases in both coin distributions and receipts. It also explains interagency collaboration on counterfeit deterrence, currency design, banknote technology, and the respective issuing authorities for notes and coins.

nodes.title: Box 5.2. U.S. Currency Program Initiatives
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve and BEP initiatives to secure, modernize, produce, and distribute U.S. currency. It covers replacement of aging processing equipment, possible regionalization of cash operations, major New York and Miami facility projects, construction of a new BEP production plant, and development of a secure and manufacturable next banknote family beginning with the $10 note in 2026. It also explains related counterfeit-resistance research, CEP education and outreach activities and 2023 performance metrics, and the Board’s cooperation with domestic and international central-bank and industry groups to protect currency integrity and maintain confidence in U.S. banknotes.

The section explains the authorities and responsibilities governing U.S. notes and coins, reviews 2023 currency and coin circulation trends, and describes Federal Reserve and BEP initiatives to modernize cash operations, facilities, production, and banknote technology. It covers development of a secure next banknote family beginning with the $10 note in 2026, counterfeit-deterrence research, Currency Education Program outreach and results, and broad interagency, central-bank, and industry cooperation to preserve currency security and public confidence.

nodes.title: Fiscal Agency and Government Depository Services
Payment Services
nodes.summary: The text explains the Federal Reserve Banks’ fiscal agency and depository roles for the Treasury and other entities, including the systems and services they provide and the associated reimbursed expenses. It presents 2021–23 expense data, then details Treasury payment services, their 2023 costs and major programs, Stored Value Card and Pay.gov operations, payment volumes and values, and the Reserve Banks’ support for Treasury financing, securities issuance and servicing, savings bonds, and 2023 Treasury auctions.

nodes.title: Financing and Securities Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank services performed for the Treasury, covering payment processing, military stored-value cards, Pay.gov, financing and securities operations, government accounting and reporting, and supporting technology infrastructure. It reports 2023 expenses, year-over-year changes and causes, major programs, and transaction volumes and values, including Treasury auctions and securities servicing. It also explains key accounting applications and identifies Treasury financial publications, with footnotes on increased securities demand, the Fedwire Securities Service change, and publication sources.

nodes.title: Accounting and Reporting Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank oversight and support for Treasury securities, accounting, reporting, and technology infrastructure. It reports 2023 securities-service expenses of $194.4 million, down 6.4% following a Fedwire Securities Service accounting change, and notes support for $427.5 billion in savings bonds and marketable securities amid a 164% rise in product demand. It explains Treasury accounting and reporting activities, including cash management and publication of key financial statements, and reports $81.1 million in related expenses, up 10.3% due mainly to technical-debt remediation, cybersecurity, and cloud migration. The Cash Accounting Reporting System and G-Invoicing are highlighted, followed by a description of Reserve Bank technology infrastructure services and referenced Treasury-report resources.

nodes.title: Infrastructure and Technology Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank services supporting Treasury securities, government accounting and reporting, technology infrastructure, and banking services for other entities, along with their 2023 expenses and year-over-year changes. It explains key systems such as the Cash Accounting Reporting System and G-Invoicing, ongoing cloud migration, automation, infrastructure modernization, and cybersecurity efforts. It also outlines the Federal Reserve's broader payment-system roles as operator, supervisor, regulator, researcher, and catalyst for improvements, and its research into payment, clearing, settlement, and financial market infrastructures. Footnotes provide explanations of Treasury-product demand, Fedwire accounting changes, official Treasury reports, and the federal Cloud Smart strategy.

nodes.title: Services Provided to Other Entities
nodes.summary: In 2023, the Reserve Banks expanded cloud migration, automation, infrastructure management, and cybersecurity, reducing infrastructure and technology expenses to $143.6 million. They also provided authorized U.S.-dollar banking and electronic securities services to other entities, with expenses falling to $14.9 million. The Federal Reserve additionally serves as a payment-system supervisor, regulator, researcher, and catalyst for improvements, studying payment, clearing, settlement, and financial market infrastructures and their role in economic activity.

The section surveys the Reserve Banks’ fiscal agency and depository services for the Treasury and other authorized entities, covering payment processing, Stored Value Cards, Pay.gov, Treasury financing and auctions, securities issuance and servicing, savings bonds, accounting and reporting, and supporting technology infrastructure. It presents expense trends through 2023, transaction volumes and values, and major year-over-year changes, including securities-service expenses of $194.4 million, accounting and reporting expenses of $81.1 million, infrastructure and technology expenses of $143.6 million, and services to other entities expenses of $14.9 million. It highlights the effects of increased Treasury-product demand, a Fedwire Securities Service accounting change, technical-debt remediation, cybersecurity, cloud migration, automation, and modernization. The section also explains systems such as the Cash Accounting Reporting System and G-Invoicing, identifies Treasury financial publications, and describes the Federal Reserve’s wider roles in operating, supervising, regulating, researching, and improving payment, clearing, settlement, and financial market infrastructures, with related explanatory footnotes and sources.

nodes.title: Evolutions and Improvements to the System
Payment System Research and Analysis
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 Reserve Bank technology investments, cloud migration, cybersecurity, and related expenses; banking, securities, and safekeeping services provided to other entities and their costs; and the Federal Reserve’s broader payment-system roles as operator, supervisor, regulator, researcher, and catalyst for improvement. It covers payment-system research on payment trends, innovations, infrastructure, and fraud; digital-innovation research involving digital assets, CBDCs, cross-border and wholesale payments; collaboration with international, governmental, academic, and private-sector stakeholders; and the Board’s statutory responsibility to implement payment- and banking-related laws through regulation.

nodes.title: Digital Innovations Research
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve research and oversight of payment systems. Its 2023 research covered payment-method trends, innovation drivers and effects, financial market infrastructure, and payments fraud. It also explains staff research into digital assets, CBDCs, cross-border and wholesale payment technologies, and the related policy, technical, risk, and infrastructure implications. The Federal Reserve works with international institutions, other central banks, and domestic stakeholders on innovations such as tokenization, distributed ledgers, APIs, and digital payments. Finally, it notes the Board’s congressional responsibility to implement payment- and banking-related laws through regulations and provides links to relevant Federal Reserve websites and the Payments Study.

nodes.title: Payment System Regulation
nodes.summary: The text reviews Federal Reserve payment-system research, digital-innovation policy and technology work, international and domestic collaboration, payment-system regulation, and major 2023 oversight actions, including proposed debit-card interchange-fee changes and creation of a public master-account database. It also describes Reserve Bank efforts to launch FedNow, modernize payment and currency-processing infrastructure, strengthen cybersecurity and operational resilience, and refresh the System IT strategy for 2024–26.

nodes.title: Other Improvements and Efforts
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 regulatory and operational developments involving the Federal Reserve’s payment systems and Reserve Banks. It covers proposed debit-card interchange-fee changes under Regulation II, the public Master Account and Services Database, FedNow implementation, technology and processing-platform modernization, currency-processing equipment replacement, IT planning and datacenter modernization, cybersecurity and resilience initiatives, facility upgrades, and references to Reserve Bank asset information. It also explains Board oversight, independent annual audits of the Reserve Banks, the Board’s reviews, and use of the COSO framework for assessing financial internal controls.

The section covers the Federal Reserve’s research, regulation, oversight, and modernization of the payment system. It describes 2023 technology, cloud, cybersecurity, infrastructure, payment-processing, and currency operations; services provided by Reserve Banks and their costs; research into payment trends, fraud, financial-market infrastructure, digital assets, CBDCs, tokenization, distributed ledgers, and cross-border and wholesale payments; and collaboration with domestic and international stakeholders. It also addresses the Board’s statutory regulatory role, major 2023 actions such as proposed debit-card interchange-fee changes and the public master-account database, FedNow implementation, IT and datacenter modernization, facility and equipment upgrades, operational resilience, Reserve Bank assets, audits, oversight, and COSO-based internal-control assessments.

nodes.title: Oversight of Federal Reserve Banks
Income and Expenses
nodes.summary: The text describes the Board’s annual oversight and external auditing of SOMA and foreign-currency operations, including FOMC compliance, technology controls, vendor management, and resiliency. It presents the Reserve Banks’ 2023 and 2022 financial results, explaining the sharp 2023 loss, the rules governing Treasury remittances and deferred assets, and the $670 million transferred in 2023. Table 5.3 details income, expenses, adjustments, losses, assessments, distributions, dividends, remittances, deferred assets, and comprehensive results, while Appendix G provides expanded financial, historical, staffing, and budget information for the Reserve Banks and related entities.

nodes.title: SOMA Holdings
nodes.summary: The text describes the FOMC-directed open market operations conducted by the New York Fed and the securities and commitments held in the SOMA, references a table comparing SOMA financial data for 2023 and 2022, reports 2023 balances and interest rates for major Reserve Bank lending programs, and notes pandemic-related SPV lending and the appendix listing Treasury and federal agency holdings.

nodes.title: Lending
nodes.summary: The text explains the FOMC-authorized open market operations conducted by the New York Fed and the securities held in SOMA, reports 2023 Reserve Bank lending balances and rates—including pandemic-related facilities and SPVs—and presents Table 5.4 comparing SOMA assets, liabilities, income, expenses, interest rates, and net holdings in 2023 and 2022. It also provides the principal asset and liability balances, changes, and income or expense results, together with definitions and valuation notes for the table's categories and a reference to Appendix G.

The section covers Reserve Bank technology, cybersecurity, and facility modernization; the Board’s oversight framework and independent audits of Reserve Bank, SOMA, foreign-currency, pandemic-related LLC, internal-control, and retirement-plan activities; COSO- and IIA-based control and internal-audit assessments; and auditor independence and fees. It also presents Reserve Bank income, expenses, losses, remittances, deferred assets, and related financial results, along with FOMC-directed New York Fed open market operations, SOMA holdings and commitments, lending programs and rates, pandemic-related facilities, and comparative SOMA financial data, with detailed tables and supporting financial, operational, staffing, budget, holdings, and property information in Appendix G.

Notes to Pro Forma Financial Statements for Priced Services

nodes.summary: The notes explain the composition and accounting treatment of short-term and long-term priced-service assets, including receivables, collection items, float costs, shared assets, deferred taxes, and Board assets. They describe the matched-book financing structure and imputed equity requirements for 2023 and 2022, note the revision to the 2022 equity percentage, and introduce the Board’s Payment System Risk policy and its reliance on international financial-market-infrastructure standards for Fedwire Services.

nodes.title: (2) Long-Term Assets
nodes.summary: The notes explain the composition and treatment of short-term and long-term priced-service assets, including receivables, collection items, float costs, deferred taxes, and Board assets. They describe the matched-book financing structure and imputed equity levels used to meet FDIC capitalization standards, note the revision to the 2022 equity figure, and introduce the Board’s Payment System Risk policy and its basis in international financial-market-infrastructure standards.

nodes.title: (3) Liabilities and Equity
nodes.summary: The notes explain the pro forma accounting for priced services, covering short- and long-term assets, float and investment assumptions, matched-book financing and imputed capital, payment-system risk requirements, pension and postretirement benefit accounting, revenues, and operating expenses. They provide the applicable equity ratios, tax rates, pension assets and funded-status effects, Board expenses, pension service costs, exclusions for FedNow development, and relevant 2022 restatements.

nodes.title: (4) Revenue
nodes.summary: The text explains Fedwire Funds Service risk-management and capital/liquidity requirements, noting that no additional imputed balances were needed in 2022 or 2023. It describes ASC 715 accounting for pension and other benefit plans, including balance-sheet recognition, deferred tax effects, AOCI impacts, pension asset amounts, and the 2023 increase in accumulated other comprehensive loss. It then defines priced-service revenue as direct fees charged to depository institutions and outlines operating expenses for Reserve Bank and Board priced-service activities, excluding FedNow development, with related Board and pension service costs. It also notes the 2019 ASC 715 disaggregation requirement and the restatement of the prior-year pension asset.

nodes.title: (5) Operating Expenses
nodes.summary: The text explains Fedwire Funds Service risk-management and pro forma capital requirements, pension accounting under ASC 715, priced-services revenue and operating expenses, pension-related costs and AOCI treatment, and the composition and tax rates of service income statements. It then describes PSAF-based imputed costs, their debt, equity, tax, sales-tax, and float assumptions and allocation, and reports 2023 and 2022 average daily credit-float recovery, including float unrelated to priced services and the definition of credit float.

nodes.title: (6) Imputed Costs
nodes.summary: The text explains Reserve Bank accounting for benefit-plan expenses, service-based income statements, imputed costs and their PSAF-based calculations, allocation of imputed debt interest, and treatment and recovery of credit float, including 2023 and 2022 recovery figures. It also covers other income from imputed investments, the cost-recovery formula, relevant float and PSAF definitions, and the applicable tax rates and accounting treatment under ASC 715.

Annual cost recovery is the ratio of revenue, including other income, to the sum of operating expenses, imputed costs, imputed income taxes, and after-tax targeted return on equity.

It details PSAF-based imputed debt, equity, taxes, investment income, targeted returns, and float assumptions, including the treatment and recovery of credit float from operational, ACH, and check-related activities. It also identifies priced-service revenues and eligible Reserve Bank and Board expenses, excludes FedNow development costs, and defines the annual cost-recovery measure incorporating revenue, other income, expenses, imputed costs and taxes, and the after-tax return on equity.

This section reports the pro forma financial position and performance of Federal Reserve priced services for 2023 and 2022, including detailed assets, liabilities, equity, revenues, expenses, imputed financing and tax costs, investment income, net income, targeted returns, and cost recovery. It also breaks down 2023 results by service and explains the accompanying accounting assumptions and notes, including PSAF-based financing, float and payment-system risk, pension and benefit accounting, taxes, eligible expenses and revenues, FedNow cost exclusions, and the 2022 pension-balance restatement.

structure.summary: This section explains how the Federal Reserve supports and oversees the U.S. payment and settlement system through priced payment services, FedNow®, currency and coin operations, Treasury fiscal and depository services, payment-system research and modernization, and comprehensive Reserve Bank oversight. It covers service operations, users, volumes, costs, revenues, pricing and cost recovery; cash production, circulation, security, and education; government payments, financing, securities, accounting, technology, and cybersecurity; regulatory, research, infrastructure, and operational-resilience initiatives; audits, internal controls, financial results, FOMC and SOMA activities, lending and pandemic facilities; and detailed 2023–22 pro forma financial statements and related accounting assumptions for priced services.

structure.title: 6 Consumer and Community Affairs

nodes.title: Consumer Compliance Supervision
Consumer Compliance Examinations
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s consumer and community affairs responsibilities, including examiner training and resources, application analysis, and consumer complaint handling. It explains consumer compliance examinations, 2023 guidance updates and HMDA reporting revisions, examination totals and institutional coverage, and the division of supervisory authority with the CFPB. It then outlines CRA requirements and implementation through examinations, application reviews, and community development outreach, reports 2023 CRA examination ratings, and notes the agencies’ issuance of a modernized CRA final rule. Finally, it introduces fair-lending and UDAP enforcement under ECOA, the Fair Housing Act, and the FTC Act, including ECOA’s prohibited bases for credit discrimination; the source text ends mid-discussion.

nodes.title: Consumer Compliance Enforcement Activities
Fair Lending and UDAP Enforcement
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 CRA supervision, including its responsibilities, 174 examinations and resulting ratings, and the agencies’ October 2023 CRA modernization rule. It then explains fair lending and consumer protection requirements under ECOA, the FHA, and the FTC Act; the respective supervisory and enforcement roles of the Federal Reserve, CFPB, and DOJ; definitions of discrimination, unfairness, and deception; enforcement and corrective-action processes; one 2023 DOJ referral involving alleged marital-status discrimination; and the Board’s compliance outreach, webinar, and publications. Finally, it outlines flood insurance requirements under the National Flood Insurance Act and Regulation H and reports a 2023 enforcement order imposing approximately $2.9455 million in penalties, distributed between FEMA and the Treasury Department.

nodes.title: Flood Insurance Enforcement
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s use of informal and public enforcement tools, its transparency and outreach efforts on fair lending and UDAP compliance—including a 2023 webinar with over 6,300 registrants and a compliance article—and its enforcement of flood insurance requirements under the National Flood Insurance Act and Regulation H. It reports a 2023 flood insurance enforcement order totaling approximately $2.9455 million, with penalties distributed to FEMA and the U.S. Treasury, and includes related reference links.

The section covers the Federal Reserve’s 2023 CRA supervision and the October 2023 CRA modernization rule; fair lending and UDAP requirements, agency responsibilities, prohibited discrimination, unfairness and deception, and related enforcement and corrective-action tools; a DOJ referral involving alleged marital-status discrimination; compliance outreach and publications; and flood insurance requirements and enforcement under the National Flood Insurance Act and Regulation H, including a 2023 order totaling approximately $2.9455 million in penalties paid to FEMA and the U.S. Treasury.

nodes.title: Mergers and Acquisitions
nodes.summary: The text explains the legal and supervisory factors the Federal Reserve considers in merger and acquisition applications, including competition, financial condition, management and compliance, CRA performance, community needs, and stability. It describes the compliance, fair-lending, supervisory, examiner, applicant, and public information used in reviews, possible pre-membership examinations, and public disclosure through Board Orders, press releases, and semiannual reports covering outcomes, processing times, withdrawals, and public comments. It also discusses 2023 coordination with the CFPB and other regulators under an interagency agreement intended to reduce burden, duplication, and conflicting directives through cooperative supervision and shared examination schedules, with footnotes linking to related guidance and reports.

nodes.title: Coordination with Other Agencies
nodes.summary: The text explains the legal and supervisory factors the Federal Reserve considers in merger and acquisition applications, including competition, financial condition, management and compliance, CRA and community needs, and financial stability. It describes the compliance, supervisory, examiner, applicant, and public information used in reviews, possible pre-membership examinations, and the Board’s public reporting through Orders, press releases, and semiannual application statistics. It also covers 2023 coordination with the CFPB and other financial regulators under an interagency agreement intended to reduce burden, duplication, and conflicting directives, including sharing examination schedules, and identifies related guidance and reporting resources.

nodes.title: Box 6.1. Supporting Consumer Protection and Community Development
Modernizing the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 efforts to support consumer protection, financial inclusion, and community development amid post-pandemic policy changes, inflation, and evolving banking technology. It describes DCCA’s regulatory, research, outreach, and risk-management work; the jointly issued modernization of CRA regulations; fair-lending education and compliance initiatives; analysis of consumer-law violations; and research from the 2022 household economic well-being survey, including its topics and related public webinar. It also provides links to referenced resources.

nodes.title: Promoting Sound Consumer Risk-Management Practices among Banks
nodes.summary: Box 6.1 of the Federal Reserve's 2023 Annual Report describes DCCA efforts to support consumer protection, financial inclusion, and community development amid the end of pandemic benefits, inflation, and banking-sector technological change. It covers the interagency modernization of CRA regulations, fair-lending and consumer-risk-management initiatives, compliance guidance on common legal violations, and research into household financial well-being and emerging consumer issues, including findings from the 2022 SHED survey and related outreach resources.

nodes.title: Conducting Research and Analysis of Emerging Consumer Issues
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer-protection and community-development work amid the end of pandemic benefits, inflation, and technological change in banking. It describes DCCA’s regulatory, research, policy, and outreach activities; the interagency modernization of CRA rules to reflect digital banking and varying bank models while supporting LMI communities; fair-lending and consumer-compliance risk-management efforts, including disability discrimination, algorithmic bias, redlining, appraisal discrimination, violation reporting, and mitigation guidance; and research on household economic well-being through the 2022 SHED survey and related webinar. It concludes with reference links to the cited resources.

nodes.title: Box 6.1—continued
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve consumer and community affairs research, outreach, and interagency supervisory coordination. Publications addressed consumer credit products, small-dollar loans, auto finance, workers’ financial well-being, student debt, food-related hardship, pandemic income trends, and women’s workforce exits. Board outreach and advisory activities examined post-pandemic economic conditions, small-business credit, housing costs, the effects of expiring COVID-19 benefits on low- and moderate-income communities, local economic recovery, and inclusive and affordable housing. The Federal Reserve also coordinates with other federal banking agencies and FFIEC members on supervisory guidance and consistent examination practices, including joint exams, information sharing, and review of examination reports, with supporting source references provided.
