nodes.title: Model Validation Council
nodes.summary:
116 110th Annual Report | 2023
Model Validation Council
The Model Validation Council was established in 2012 by the Board of Governors to provide expert and independent advice on its process to rigorously assess the models used in stress tests of banking institutions. The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act required the Federal Reserve to conduct annual stress tests of large bank holding companies and systemically important, nonbank financial institutions supervised by the Board. The Model Validation Council provides input on the Board’s efforts to assess the effectiveness of the models used in the stress tests. The council is intended to improve the quality of the Federal Reserve’s model assessment program and to strengthen the confidence in the integrity and independence of the program.
Members
The council had no members or meetings during 2023.

nodes.summary: The text explains the Board’s expense-monitoring and variance-review processes and summarizes budget, operating-expense, staffing, and capital-spending tables for 2023–24, including OIG information. The Board spent slightly above its 2023 operating authority, underspent single-year capital, and overspent multiyear capital because of early construction while remaining within projected project totals. It provides operating-area and organizational-unit results, explains special accounts and the Survey of Consumer Finances, notes the effects of the July 2023 cost-accounting framework, and describes the $1.0441 billion 2024 operating budget, which is 5.0 percent above 2023 actual expenses and supports five organizational goal areas.

nodes.title: 2024 Operating Expense Budget
nodes.summary: The text presents the Federal Reserve Board’s 2023–24 operating, staffing, and capital budgets. It details divisional and account-level operating expenses, 2023 budget-to-actual variances, 2024 budget increases, OIG finances, benefits and special accounts, authorized positions, and explanatory notes on the Survey of Consumer Finances and position accounting. Board operations totaled $994.1 million in 2023 actual expenses against a $989.6 million budget, with a $1,044.1 million 2024 budget. The 2024 budget supports compensation, strategic hiring, contractors, ongoing services, and priority initiatives, while capital plans include a $25.1 million single-year program and $364.3 million in expected multiyear-project expenditures focused on equipment, software, facilities, security, modernization, collaboration, efficiency, productivity, and sustainability.

nodes.title: 2024 Capital Budgets
nodes.summary: The text presents Board staffing authorizations for 2023 and 2024, including division-level budgets, year-end actuals, variances, and totals. Board operations remain at 2,990 positions in 2023 and rise to 3,007 in 2024, while the Inspector General and Currency functions also expand. It defines budget versus actual position counts and identifies the extraordinary-items pool. The text then describes the 2024 capital budgets: a $25.1 million single-year budget, elevated by deferred 2023 purchases, and $364.3 million in expected multiyear capital spending focused on building improvements and a secure, modern, efficient, collaborative, productive, and sustainable work environment.

nodes.title: Office of Inspector General
nodes.summary: The text explains the OIG's independent, strategic-plan-based budgeting process and reports its 2023 budget performance and 2024 operating and capital budgets. It details actual and budgeted operating income, expenses, and capital spending, explains the main variances and 2024 budget increases, identifies planned capital projects, and references Tables D.5 and D.7 and the OIG strategic plan.

nodes.title: 2023 Budget Performance
nodes.summary: The text describes the OIG’s strategically aligned and independently prepared budget process, reports that 2023 operating expenses met budget while operating income exceeded projections due partly to increased CFPB work, and notes lower-than-budgeted capital spending. It then presents the 2024 operating and capital budgets, explaining their increases and planned uses, and references the relevant budget tables and OIG strategic plan.

nodes.title: 2024 Operating Expense Budget
nodes.summary: The text explains the OIG's strategic-plan-based, independently prepared budgeting process and reports its 2023 budget performance and 2024 budgets. In 2023, operating expenses excluding income matched the $54.1 million budget, operating income exceeded budget by $3.3 million, CFPB-related activity contributed to total expenses of $34.6 million including CFPB income, and capital spending was $0.1 million, or 54.6 percent, below budget. The 2024 operating budget is $59.0 million excluding CFPB income and $39.0 million including it, reflecting staffing, compensation, benefits, and vacancy-rate changes. The 2024 capital budget is $0.5 million for vehicles, equipment, and San Francisco office improvements, with referenced tables providing budget and actual figures.

nodes.title: 2024 Capital Budget
nodes.summary: The text explains the OIG’s strategically grounded and independently prepared budget, presents its 2023 operating and capital performance, details the 2024 operating and capital budgets and staffing increase, and summarizes Board and OIG capital expenditures and variances in Table D.7. It then describes how Federal Reserve Banks set and monitor strategically aligned goals, organize budgets around their core monetary-policy, financial-stability, supervision, and service responsibilities, and begin a budget process involving a simplified five-committee structure led by the Conferences of Presidents and First Vice Presidents.

The section explains how the Federal Reserve Board and its Office of Inspector General develop, monitor, and report strategically aligned operating, staffing, and capital budgets. It covers 2023 budget performance and variances, detailed organizational and account-level results, cost-accounting changes, staffing authorizations, special accounts, and the Survey of Consumer Finances; presents the Board’s $1.0441 billion 2024 operating budget and $25.1 million single-year and $364.3 million multiyear capital plans; and describes the OIG’s independent budgeting process, 2023 results, $59.0 million 2024 operating budget excluding CFPB income, $39.0 million including it, and $0.5 million capital budget. It also defines capital-budget coverage, references the relevant tables and strategic plans, and outlines the Reserve Banks’ strategic budgeting responsibilities and simplified committee-based process.

nodes.title: Federal Reserve Banks Budgets
2023 Budget Performance
nodes.summary: The text presents Federal Reserve Bank operating expense budgets and actuals by account for 2023–24. Actual 2023 expenses were essentially on budget at $5,648.3 million, with variances driven by modernization, staffing, and facility-related costs, while staffing and capital expenditures were below plan. The 2024 budget rises to $6,053.2 million, mainly because of expanded inflation-related monetary policy work and Treasury fees, software, personnel, and vendor support. Account definitions, pension exclusions, other-expense components, and the Board’s approval of the 2024 budget are also provided.

nodes.title: 2024 Operating Expense Budget
nodes.summary: The text presents Federal Reserve System budget and staffing statistics for 2023–24. It details Reserve Bank operating expenses by account, showing $5.6483 billion in 2023 actual expenses—slightly above the $5.6462 billion budget—and a $6.0532 billion 2024 budget, driven by inflation research, Treasury and technology needs, NextGen cash initiatives, supervision growth, and FedNow investments. It explains the main sources of 2023 variances, staffing performance, personnel-cost increases, and salary and variable-pay programs. Employment tables provide District, National IT, and Office of Employee Benefits staffing data, totaling 20,680 actual FTEs in 2023 and 21,238 budgeted for 2024. Capital-expenditure tables show $645.5 million spent in 2023 against an $888.2 million budget and a $913.8 million 2024 budget, supporting IT, cash services, buildings, NextGen, and data-center modernization. The text also includes definitions, organizational notes, approval and budget footnotes, and conditional approval of $334.2 million in 2024 projects.

nodes.title: 2024 Capital Budgets
nodes.summary: The text presents a district-by-district table of Federal Reserve and National IT capital budgets and variances for 2023 and 2024, showing total 2023 actual expenditures of $645.5 million and a 2024 budget of $913.8 million. It explains related salary and variable-pay programs, the purposes of the 2024 capital budget, conditional-approval projects, other large and small capital initiatives, and the currency budget, including BEP note-production reimbursements, currency distribution, security, issuance, and statutory funding responsibilities.

This section explains Federal Reserve System and Reserve Bank budgeting, covering Board and OIG capital expenditures, Reserve Bank strategic functions, governance and approval procedures, monitoring, and capital-project review. It presents 2023 budgeted versus actual and 2024 budgeted operating expenses by District, operating area, and account, together with explanations of variances, inclusions, exclusions, staffing, personnel costs, salary and variable-pay programs, and employment totals. It also details Reserve Bank capital budgets and projects, including IT, cash, facilities, NextGen, data-center, FedNow, and modernization initiatives, conditional approvals, and currency-production and distribution responsibilities, while identifying the supporting tables, definitions, organizational notes, and statistical references.

nodes.title: Currency Budget
2023 Budget Performance
nodes.summary: The text explains how the Federal Reserve’s currency budget supports banknote production quality, anti-counterfeiting work, currency integrity, and public education; outlines the annual budget-development and approval process; reviews 2023 BEP and Board budget performance, including the effect of a reimbursement credit and the causes of underruns; and presents the 2024 single-cycle budget of $1.104 billion, with detailed BEP, Board, and program-category amounts and notes on reimbursement reconciliation and included costs.

nodes.title: 2024 Budget
BEP Single-Cycle Operating Costs
nodes.summary: The text reports the composition of the BEP operating budget, details 2023–24 funding and historical spending for three multicycle capital projects—including their approval history—and describes the 2024 single-cycle operating budget, including fixed and variable printing costs, their year-over-year increases, and the factors driving those changes. The three multicycle projects have a combined lifetime budget of $3,331.9 million.

nodes.title: BEP Multicycle Project Operating Costs
nodes.summary: The text details the Federal Reserve's 2024 currency budget, covering BEP single-cycle operating costs, multicycle capital projects, and Board expenses. BEP single-cycle costs are budgeted at $1,033.7 million, with increases in fixed and variable printing costs driven by technology, cybersecurity, staffing, deliveries, and materials. Three multicycle projects—Fort Worth expansion, the Washington, D.C. replacement facility, and note-production equipment modernization—have a combined lifetime budget of $3,331.9 million, with specified approved, conditional, prior-year, 2023, and 2024 funding. The text also explains project purposes and 2024 allocations, presents the revised historical-cost basis in Figure D.4, and reports a $70.2 million Board operating budget, with increases tied to strategic initiatives, currency distribution, banknote development, security testing, usability, and design-process improvements.

nodes.title: Board Single-Cycle Operating Costs
nodes.summary: The text details Federal Reserve currency-related multicycle and single-cycle budgets. It gives approved and conditional funding for WCF and DCRF facilities and BEP note-production equipment, including 2024 project allocations and equipment life expectations. It describes the currency-cost figure and its methodology, reports the Board's $70.2 million 2024 operating budget and year-over-year increase, and explains higher costs for currency issuance and banknote development. It also outlines currency-education priorities, two added positions, and the personnel, travel, training, and enterprise support costs included in the currency budget.

The section presents the Federal Reserve’s 2024 currency budget, covering BEP printing and support operations, three multicycle capital projects, and Board currency-related expenses. It explains 2023 BEP and Board budget variances, the $1,033.7 million 2024 BEP budget and its cost drivers, and the three projects’ combined $3,331.9 million lifetime budget, funding history, purposes, allocations, and cost methodology. It also details the Board’s $70.2 million 2024 budget, including higher issuance, development, security, usability, education, staffing, and enterprise-support costs. The total 2024 single-cycle currency budget is $1,104.0 million, $180.3 million above 2023 actual expenses, with itemized variances shown in Table D.13.

The section first outlines related capital expenditures and then explains how the Federal Reserve’s Currency Budget finances BEP banknote production and the Board’s statutory currency-issuing responsibilities, including supply, quality, security, transportation, resilience, and public education. It reviews the 2023 budgeting and performance results, including credits, underruns, and reconciliations, and presents the 2024 $1.104 billion single-cycle budget: $1,033.7 million for BEP operations and three multicycle capital projects totaling $3,331.9 million over their lifetimes, and $70.2 million for Board currency activities. It also details the projects, cost drivers, staffing and program expenses, and the principal variances from 2023 actual spending.

structure.summary: This section provides a comprehensive overview of Federal Reserve System operating and capital budgets, accountability, performance, strategic priorities, governance, and approval processes. It compares 2023 budgeted and actual results and presents detailed 2024 budgets for the Board, OIG, Reserve Banks, and currency operations, including expenses, staffing, personnel and compensation programs, revenues, reimbursements, accounting, organizational changes, and capital plans. It discusses long-term cost and employment trends and major initiatives such as technology and payment modernization, FedNow, Fedwire, ACH, NextGen, facilities, data centers, and currency infrastructure. It also explains Reserve Bank and Board budget monitoring and project review, and details the Currency Budget’s support for BEP production and the Board’s statutory responsibilities, including its 2024 funding, multiyear capital projects, performance variances, and operational priorities.

structure.title: E Record of Policy Actions of the Board of Governors

nodes.title: Rules and Regulations
Regulation BB (Community Reinvestment)
nodes.summary: The text summarizes two Board regulatory actions reported in the 2023 Annual Report: a joint CRA rule that modernizes community reinvestment evaluations through tiered requirements, lending and community-development metrics, expanded geographic coverage, and clarified qualifying activities, along with a later rule extending certain implementation dates and making technical amendments; and a joint update to administrative procedure rules recognizing electronic communications and improving adjudication efficiency and fairness. It states effective dates, participating agencies, docket numbers, voting records, and related Federal Register references.

nodes.title: Rules of Practice and Procedure
nodes.summary: The text summarizes 2023 Federal Reserve regulatory and policy actions. It covers the modernization of Community Reinvestment Act regulations and subsequent applicability-date amendments; electronic updates to administrative hearing procedures; revised allowances-for-credit-loss guidance removing TDR references; updated guidance for commercial real estate loan accommodations and workouts; and a Section 9(13) policy establishing consistent limits on bank activities, including crypto-related activities, while emphasizing legal compliance, safety, soundness, risk management, and internal controls. It also records effective dates, interagency participation, voting outcomes, and related Federal Register notices.

This section records the Federal Reserve Board’s 2023 policy actions pursuant to the Federal Reserve Act, explaining the reporting framework, action categories, voting records, source materials, and relationship to FOMC actions. It summarizes capital requirements for holding companies engaged in insurance, including the Building Block Approach, as well as Community Reinvestment Act modernization and implementation amendments, electronic administrative-procedure updates, credit-loss and commercial-real-estate workout guidance, and limits on bank activities under Section 9(13), including crypto-related activities. The section also notes the relevant statutory purposes, effective dates, agencies, dockets, votes, and Federal Register references.

nodes.title: Policy Statements and Other Actions
Allowances for Credit Losses
nodes.summary: The text records three Board policy actions in 2023: an interagency allowances-for-credit-losses statement removing obsolete TDR references after CECL-related accounting changes; updated interagency guidance on commercial real estate loan workouts and short-term accommodations for financially stressed but creditworthy borrowers; and a section 9(13) policy generally aligning state member bank activity limits with those for national banks, including for novel activities such as crypto-assets, while emphasizing legal compliance, safety, soundness, risk management, and internal controls. Each action received unanimous approval from Chair Powell, Vice Chair Barr, and Governors Bowman, Waller, Cook, and Jefferson, with Federal Register citations provided.

nodes.title: Commercial Real Estate Loan Accommodations and Workouts
nodes.summary: The text records three Board policy actions in 2023: an interagency update removing Troubled Debt Restructuring references from allowances-for-credit-loss guidance following CECL-related accounting changes; updated interagency guidance on commercial real estate loan workouts and short-term accommodations during borrower financial stress; and a section 9(13) policy statement generally aligning state member bank activity limits with those for national banks, including restrictions on novel and crypto-asset-related activities. The latter emphasizes legal compliance, safe and sound operations, risk management, and internal controls. The first two actions were jointly issued with the FDIC, OCC, and NCUA, Federal Register citations are provided, and the listed votes for them were unanimous among the named Board members.

nodes.title: Policy Statement on Section 9(13) of the Federal Reserve Act
nodes.summary: The excerpt records Federal Reserve Board policy actions in 2023 concerning credit-loss allowances, commercial real estate workouts and short-term accommodations, interpretation of section 9(13) and uniform limits on bank activities, climate-related financial risk management, and emergency measures following the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank. It explains the purpose and scope of each policy, identifies interagency partners and applicable institutions, provides voting outcomes, describes the systemic-risk exception and Bank Term Funding Program authorities, and supplies official source references.

nodes.title: Principles for Climate-Related Financial Risk Management
nodes.summary: The excerpt covers requirements for appropriate information systems; Board voting on a related action; approval of interagency climate-related financial risk principles for institutions with over $100 billion in assets, including physical and transition risks and the vote split; and the Board's March 12, 2023 response to the SVB and Signature Bank failures. That response involved recommending the systemic risk exception to normal FDIC least-cost resolution rules and establishing the emergency Bank Term Funding Program under section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act. It explains the banks' receiverships, deposit runs, financial-stability rationale, and the statutory conditions and limitations governing the program, with supporting footnote references.

nodes.title: Systemic Risk Exception and Bank Term Funding Program
nodes.summary: The text records Board actions on information-system adequacy, climate-related financial risk principles, emergency responses to the 2023 failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, and third-party risk management. It explains the systemic risk exception and the Bank Term Funding Program’s legal basis, eligibility, collateral, pricing, later rate modification, and scheduled closure, and gives the voting outcomes for each action, including dissenting governors and supporting source references.

nodes.title: Third-Party Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text records Board actions involving requirements for securing loans to insolvent entities, establishment and later modification and scheduled termination of the BTFP, including its eligibility, collateral, advance terms, valuation, and interest rate, as well as the votes approving those actions. It also describes final interagency third-party risk-management guidance issued with the FDIC and OCC, its purpose and principles, the related votes, and referenced source documents.

nodes.title: Interest on Reserves
nodes.summary: The 2023 record details the Board’s reserve-balance interest-rate decisions: increases from 4.4% to 5.4% between February and July, followed by maintenance at 5.4% from September through December, each aligned with corresponding FOMC federal funds target-range actions and accompanied by voting records and press-release citations. It also explains the statutory and biweekly process for setting discount-window rates for depository institutions, including primary, secondary, and seasonal credit rates, and points to year-end rate tables and online historical references.

This section records the Federal Reserve Board’s 2023 policy statements and related actions on credit-loss allowances, commercial real estate accommodations and workouts, state member bank activity limits under section 9(13), climate-related financial risk management, emergency measures following the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, third-party risk management, interest on reserve balances, and discount-window rates. It explains the purposes, legal authorities, scope, eligibility, risk controls, and operational terms of these policies, including the systemic-risk exception and Bank Term Funding Program, and provides voting results, dissenting views, interagency participation, and official citations and references.

nodes.title: Discount Rates for Depository Institutions in 2023
Primary, Secondary, and Seasonal Credit
nodes.summary: The text presents year-end 2023 Federal Reserve lending rates and explains the eligibility, purpose, pricing, and operational terms of primary, secondary, and seasonal credit. It records four primary-rate increases from 4.5% to 5.5%, a 50-basis-point secondary-credit spread, and a 5.35% seasonal rate, along with the Board’s renewal of rate-calculation formulas. It then introduces the 2023 votes and FOMC meeting details concerning discount-rate changes, beginning with the February 1 meeting, whose list of approving Reserve Banks and actions is cut off in the excerpt.

nodes.title: Votes on Changes to Discount Rates for Depository Institutions
nodes.summary: The text presents year-end 2023 Federal Reserve lending rates and explains the purposes, eligibility, terms, and rate-setting methods for primary, secondary, and seasonal credit. It records four Board-approved increases in the primary credit rate—from 4.5% to 5.5% between February and July 2023—along with the participating Reserve Banks, effective dates, and governors voting for each action. It also notes the 50-basis-point secondary-credit spread, the seasonal-credit calculation and year-end rate, renewal of the secondary and seasonal rate formulas, the 90-day renewable primary-credit borrowing provision, and a related 2020 press-release reference.

The section records the Board's September, November, and December 2023 decisions to maintain the reserve-balances rate at 5.4 percent in support of an unchanged 5¼-to-5½-percent federal funds target range, including the voting records. It explains the statutory and procedural framework for setting discount-window rates and summarizes the eligibility, purposes, pricing, formulas, and operating terms of primary, secondary, and seasonal credit. It reports four primary-credit-rate increases from 4.5 percent to 5.5 percent between February and July, the 50-basis-point secondary-credit spread, the 5.35 percent year-end seasonal rate, renewed calculation formulas, renewable primary-credit borrowing for up to 90 days, year-end rates in table E.1, and the recorded Reserve Bank actions and Board votes, beginning with an incomplete February 1 entry. The section also cites related press releases, meeting minutes, and discount-rate resources.

nodes.title: The Board of Governors and the Government Performance and Results Act
nodes.summary: The Board voluntarily follows the GPRA framework by publishing a multiyear strategic plan, annual performance plan, and annual performance report. Its 2020–23 strategic plan establishes priorities across five functional areas, while the annual plan allocates projects and resources to support those priorities and the annual report records progress and accomplishments. These processes guide mission-critical work, allow flexibility for emerging challenges, and promote public transparency; the documents are available on the Board’s website.

structure.summary: This section records the Federal Reserve Board’s 2023 rules, regulations, policy statements, emergency and supervisory actions, discount-rate decisions, and related legal, procedural, voting, interagency, and citation information. It covers capital and banking-activity requirements, CRA modernization, administrative procedures, credit-loss and commercial-real-estate guidance, climate and third-party risk management, responses to bank failures, reserve remuneration, and the terms and rates of discount-window credit. It also describes the Board’s strategic planning, performance planning, and reporting under the GPRA framework and the transparency of those processes.

structure.title: F Litigation
structure.summary: The text reports the Board of Governors’ 2023 litigation activity: 16 total cases, comprising 7 new and 9 previously pending matters, with 11 still pending at year-end, matching the 2022 total. It lists pending cases involving master-account access, breach of contract and debt collection, Regulation II debit interchange fees, bank-acquisition approval, and Freedom of Information Act requests, and describes five resolved matters, including stipulated dismissals, dismissal of a Regulation II challenge, and appellate affirmance of the Board’s prohibition orders.

structure.title: G Statistical Tables
structure.summary: Appendix G of the 2023 Annual Report compiles 13 statistical tables covering Federal Reserve open market operations; securities holdings and temporary transactions; reserve requirements; U.S. banking offices and bank-holding-company affiliations; reserve-fund supply and absorption data from 1918 through 2023; commercial-bank assets and liabilities; historical margin requirements; the statements of condition of all Reserve Banks; Reserve Bank income, expenses, remittances, and comprehensive income; operational processing volumes; personnel and salaries; and Reserve Bank premises costs and book values. Detailed notes explain classifications, valuation, accounting changes, regulatory history, rounding, unavailable data, and related Federal Reserve sources.
